data.title: Stanford Endowment Soars with SpaceX (SPCX)
data.description:
The endowment fund of Harvard surged to a record $68 billion as successful bets on equities and venture capital, including SpaceX (SPCX), helped the richest U.S. college handle an unprecedented pressure campaign from Washington, D.C.

Harvard’s endowment fund returned 27% as donations also rose to $1.5 billion, according to a financial report for the fiscal year ending in June.

These strong gains in the stock market and its hedge fund portfolio allowed Harvard to easily beat the 19% median return before fees for large U.S. college endowments and post its best year since 2021.

But wait. Stanford University, with a 32% return, beat Harvard handily, and the University of Pennsylvania basically tied its performance.

Heading one of these endowments is a hot seat. Harvard’s fund chief is N.P. “Narv” Narvekar, who has been in place for a decade, is ending his career on a high note and has apparently faced some criticism for some investments in private equity.

Endowment gains are crucial to universities as they contend with uncertainty around future government research funding. Cutting costs is also part of the deal; Harvard, for one, froze employee pay.

All the above schools had a solid year due to skilled and perhaps lucky asset allocation with the global perspective that these endowments employ.

What can we learn from these endowments about investing?

[text_ad]

While most individual investors focus on short-term stock picks and chase funds with the highest latest returns, endowments put their energies and resources into asset allocation. By this I mean figuring out what percentage of their capital to put in different buckets of assets such as U.S. or international large-cap and small-cap stocks, real estate, timber, precious metals, energy, different countries, venture capital and private equity.

A key difference is the variety of buckets endowments use to diversify, with the goals of lowering risk and volatility and increasing returns.

Endowment investment returns are critical, as Harvard provided more than $775 million in financial aid and spent $969 million on capital expenditures. Roughly 40% of the university’s operating revenue comes from the endowment.

One edge these endowments have over us mortals is a high allocation to private equity, which grew to 46%. Still, the university maintains significant liquid assets and access to credit lines to supercharge financial flexibility.

Another advantage is that endowments get opportunities to invest in private companies way before they go public. Early-stage investors get in on the game at much lower prices, thus boosting returns considerably as the companies go public. After all, it was a no-brainer that SpaceX would go public at some point.

Stanford may have an edge on Harvard due to its proximity to Silicon Valley and its legions of alumni who become tech mavens, executives, and investors.

Finally, while Harvard held $2 billion in SpaceX shares as of June 3, early investments in SpaceX have fueled stellar gains at a handful of other endowments, with the University of North Carolina and Washington University posting returns of more than 35% in the most recent fiscal year. I’m sure there are others that did even better, but perhaps they took on more risk?

Endowment returns, like our own, must be evaluated on returns over time as well as year-to-year volatility. One great year cannot be followed by a loser. Even a ten-year time frame is too short.

I would love to know what asset classes, stocks, and funds these endowments are after next. We can all benefit from having the patience and discipline to follow the endowment model.

[author_ad]

data.title: Dick’s Sporting Goods (DKS) Stock a Buy as Shares Go on Sale
data.description:
Shoppers always love a good sale.

Insiders at big retail chains do, as well.

At Dick’s Sporting Goods (DKS), directors, officers and the chief financial officer have been loading up on their company’s stock in its big pullback. In the 42%-off sale on Dick’s shares since late June, these insiders have purchased $5.6 million worth of stock at prices up to 136.39.

You can still purchase the stock at prices not much above the upper end of their buy range, and it looks like it makes sense to do so.

[text_ad]

Why Dick’s Sporting Goods (DKS) Stock Is on Sale Now

The stock is down due to weak sales at its recently acquired Foot Locker chain. However, this is a fixable problem. Dick’s management has a decent track record of turning around their core retail chain. Now they are betting they can do the same at Foot Locker.

Foot Locker sales are weak in part because shoppers have fallen out of love with Nike, a heavily stocked shoe brand at Foot Locker.

While second-quarter comparable sales rose 4.9% at Dick’s stores (69% of sales), they slid 3.6% at Foot Locker (31%). Overall operating margin fell to 7.9% from 12.4%. Non-GAAP 2026 EPS guidance was cut to $11-$12 from $13.50-$14.50.

Investors have been selling because it looks like Dick’s Foot Locker purchase was a mistake, even though it paid only 0.3 times sales. Foot Locker’s problems are also linked to inventory clear-outs in the sportswear space overall. And Foot Locker has a lot of exposure to lower-income consumers and Europe, where consumer demand has softened.

How Dick’s Management Can Engineer a Turnaround

In short, Foot Locker is broken, which makes it a turnaround candidate. Dick’s management can boost Foot Locker sales with new merchandising, store remodeling, and brand-building advertising. Over the past few years, Dick’s has increased its own operating margins to above 10% from the mid-single digits, thanks to improved merchandising, remodeled stores, and digital capabilities. It can apply the same magic to Foot Locker.

Here are some other positives to the story.

* Dick’s has strong brand and customer loyalty. The chain offers a vast, on-trend product assortment and a good in-store experience. It has roughly 30 million ScoreCard loyalty members. They account for more than 75% of the company’s sales. Vendors like the chain because of the reach it offers and the store-within-a-store model to showcase products.

* Dick’s benefits from its House of Sport store concept (giant stores with popular offerings like climbing walls, batting cages and even ice rinks) and its GameChanger app for youth sports. GameChanger enhances consumer engagement and strengthens its database by offering consumers a platform to watch games, track statistics and interact.

* Insiders buying their own turnaround is often a profitable dynamic in investing. At Dick’s the insider buy signal is strong. These qualities enhance the insider signal. They are buying in size (the $5.6 million). This is a cluster buy. Seven insiders have purchased. There is C-suite buying, since the CFO purchased.

The bottom line: Insiders bought a lot of stock at prices up to 136.39. Consider buying now as a bet that Dick’s can get Foot Locker in shape. This is also a good candidate for put selling for income. The extreme stock price compression and insider buying in the low-to-mid-130s suggest, but do not guarantee, that further dramatic price declines (the big negative in put shorting) are less likely. Also consider owning for the decent 3.5% yield. Note that turnarounds take time. You should only consider buying as a multi-year hold.

For more stocks that look promising because of exceptional insider buying, consider subscribing to Cabot Insider Edge here.

data.title: What Investors Should Expect from the Fed Today
data.description:
The outcome of today’s Federal Reserve decision should be one of the easiest ones to predict this year.

The CME FedWatch Tool currently puts the probability that the Fed holds rates steady at about 90%, versus just a 10% chance of another quarter-point hike.

That’s a dramatic shift from only a month ago, when markets were pricing in a 64% probability of an October hike.

So, what changed?

It’s certainly not that the inflation problem has evaporated like the glorious days of summer (where did it go?).

September CPI accelerated to 3.7% from 3.4% in August, while core PCE, the Fed’s preferred inflation gauge, is still running around 3%. That’s well above the Fed’s 2% target.
Still, rather than being in a rush to hike, the Fed seems to think it has the luxury of time.

September payrolls increased by just 29,000, providing little evidence that the labor market is overheating. And since September’s 25-basis-point hike, Fed officials have repeatedly indicated they don’t need to raise rates again immediately.

That means the message for investors today is likely to be a pause. But don’t mistake it for a pivot.

[text_ad]

The Fed Isn’t Done Fighting Inflation

There’s still a strong case for additional tightening after the October meeting.

Economic growth remains resilient, the AI investment boom continues to drive capital spending, and inflation has proven to be persistently stubborn.

J.P. Morgan economists recently quantified just how much the Fed’s tone has changed. Their proprietary Hawk-Dove Score for U.S. policymakers recently stood at +33.6, up from just +5.0 one month ago. Since higher scores indicate more hawkish commentary, that’s a significant shift toward inflation fighting and additional tightening, even if it doesn’t happen today.

That said, J.P. Morgan expects a shallow hiking cycle, not an aggressive tightening campaign like 2022. While inflation has remained sticky, analysts at the bank believe that energy and some technology-related input-cost pressures will ease, reducing some of the recent upward pressure on prices.

So, today’s meeting isn’t really about whether or not a quarter-point hike matters right now. It’s about Warsh convincing investors that the Fed remains serious about inflation, without raising fears that a series of economy-crushing hikes is coming.

For small-cap investors, there’s another number I’ll be watching even more closely than the fed funds rate.

Small Caps Need the 10-Year to Behave

The 10-year Treasury yield surged through September and early October, eventually reaching roughly 5.36% before retreating back toward 5%.

That move had a major impact on small caps.

The S&P 600 peaked above 1,830 in August, then rolled over as long-term rates surged, falling to about 1,640 in mid-October.

The pullback in smaller companies – which was much more severe than in large caps – is not surprising. Smaller companies typically have fewer financing options and feel higher borrowing costs more directly. Higher Treasury yields also make shares of small-cap stocks less attractive relative to bonds.

The good news is that the 10-year has stopped going straight up.

As yields have stabilized around 5%, the S&P 600 has also stabilized around the 1,690 level. It is back above its 200- and 25-day moving average lines, and knocking on the door of its 50-day line.

Small-cap investors take note: Today’s bond-market reaction may ultimately matter more than the widely expected Fed decision itself. If Warsh strikes the right balance and the 10-year remains around current levels, or moves lower, the odds of small caps continuing to recover go up.

[author_ad]

data.title: Preparing for a Post-Election Stock Market Rally
data.description:
With the 2026 midterm elections just around the corner, investors are wondering what comes next for the stock market.

Although the major indexes have held up relatively well, weakness beneath the surface, rising interest rates and renewed uncertainty surrounding AI stocks have made investors increasingly cautious.

But that uncertainty could also be setting the stage for a post-election stock market rally.

Historically, the stock market has often performed well in the months following midterm elections, as political uncertainty fades and investors turn their attention back to corporate earnings, economic growth and company fundamentals.

Could a similar pattern unfold this year?

Four Cabot analysts recently shared their perspectives on the market and the opportunities they’re watching as the midterms approach. And while each highlights a number of near-term challenges, all four believe there are reasons to remain optimistic about the months ahead.

[text_ad]

Pre-Midterm Market Weakness Could Set the Stage for a Fourth-Quarter Rally

According to Cabot turnaround investing expert Clif Droke, the stock market may be in a better position than it appears. Although the major indexes haven’t suffered especially steep declines, many individual stocks have experienced significant corrections.

That weakness, combined with the potential for seasonal strength following the midterm elections, could create an attractive environment for investors.

Clif explains:

As we head into the midterms, if you look at the major indexes, it doesn’t appear that there’s been much of a pullback. But below the surface, we’ve had something of an internal correction.

About 40% of large-cap stocks are down 25%, and 25% of S&P 500 stocks are down 40% from their highs.

I think that puts the market in a pretty good position once we get past this pre-midterm weakness and the typical fourth-quarter seasonal strength presumably kicks in.

Clif also sees potential opportunities emerging in sectors that are reversing periods of underperformance.

One of the areas of strength right now is healthcare. It’s one of the hottest-performing sectors and has done well for us at the Turnaround Letter.

While there were some excellent turnaround opportunities in healthcare heading into this quarter, it’s becoming more of a momentum trade.

Where I see turnaround potential heading further into this quarter and next year is aerospace and defense stocks, which are down significantly from this year’s highs.

Capital spending among defense contractors is expected to increase significantly next year as geopolitical activity presumably picks up, probably at some point after the midterms. That, in turn, should push inflation higher as well.

Clif also points to the massive investment in artificial intelligence as another potential catalyst for gold.

With AI hyperscaler bond issuance expected to double this year and next year, there’s a lot of concern about a potential credit bubble forming in the AI space.

That, in turn, could cause investors to seek higher-quality government bonds, such as U.S. Treasuries, which would push down Treasury yields. And that’s typically bullish for gold prices as well.

I see a lot of potential catalysts for higher gold prices.

For investors preparing for the post-election market, Clif’s outlook suggests that gold and gold mining companies could benefit from economic and geopolitical developments even if the broader stock market remains volatile.

Could Bearish Sentiment Fuel a Post-Election Stock Market Rally?

Cabot options expert Jacob Mintz sees another potentially encouraging development: Institutional investors are continuing to make bullish bets across a variety of sectors.

The basis of my system is tracking unusual options activity. I’m looking for where hedge funds and institutions are putting their big money to work.

The trend over the last couple of days, although [October 22 was] a little dicey, has been big call buying in AI names, banks, consumer stocks and restaurant stocks. There’s widespread call buying across many sectors, and that’s something I really like to see.

In terms of confidence, hedge funds and institutions are putting big money to work.

That buying activity stands in contrast to the recent performance of growth stocks, particularly those tied to artificial intelligence.

The AI trade is getting rocky. There are definitely some questions about growth stocks and AI.

Since the start of November 2025, consumer staples have outperformed the Nasdaq by nearly 10 percentage points. That’s a pretty shocking statistic. Everyone thinks AI stocks and semiconductors have been so hot, but in reality, there have been a lot of questions about those groups.

Jacob believes that skepticism could eventually work in investors’ favor, particularly if market conditions improve after the midterms.

I think that coming out of the election, once that decision has been made, and as we get closer to year-end, if the market can turn, there could be an epic chase higher.

Traders have been bearish, or at least marginally bearish, on these stocks and the market. If we start to see the stock market move higher and higher, investors could begin chasing those gains.

In other words, the same negative sentiment that’s weighed on growth stocks could help fuel a rebound if investors become more optimistic.

And that possibility isn’t limited to the largest technology companies.

Small-Cap Stocks Could Offer Opportunities Beyond the Major Indexes

Cabot small-cap investing expert Tyler Laundon sees reasons for cautious optimism as well.

Although higher interest rates have weighed on smaller companies, Tyler points out that small-cap stocks have actually held up better than many investors might realize.

Looking at the big picture, I’m cautiously optimistic about the market, but not bearish.

The economic data we’re continuing to get looks pretty good by and large. Certainly, there are some issues out there, but with third-quarter earnings season getting underway, I think we’re going to see attention shift away from macroeconomic events and back toward corporate growth and company fundamentals.

That’s a lot of what powered the strong market toward the end of the summer.

Tyler acknowledges that interest rates remain an important consideration, especially for smaller companies that tend to be more sensitive to borrowing costs.

Higher rates have definitely hurt the group. The S&P 600 SmallCap Index peaked back in August and has been trying to stabilize around its 200-day moving average.

But beneath the surface, the performance data shows that even though small caps have pulled back substantially since their August highs, they’re still leading year to date.

Small caps are up about 14.5%, versus roughly 12% for the S&P 500. So they’re still modestly ahead despite the sharp interest rate increase in August.

That relative strength suggests investors shouldn’t overlook smaller companies simply because of volatility.

Some of the market’s best growth stories are happening below the mega-cap level. Mega-cap stocks get all the news and attention, but there are a lot of other stories that aren’t being told.

It would be wrong to say that small- and mid-cap stocks aren’t working simply because their indexes took a dive in August and September when interest rates surged.

Higher financing costs and valuation multiples matter more for smaller companies. But we’re now seeing the 10-year Treasury yield pull back a little.

Rather than focusing exclusively on the direction of the broader market, Tyler is looking for specific characteristics that could help individual companies outperform.

What I’m looking for in small- and mid-cap stocks is pretty simple: improving fundamentals and identifiable growth catalysts that will be reflected in the share price when investors learn about them.

Ideally, we’re looking for operating leverage or cash generation so that as these catalysts take place, profit margins are expanding.

And, of course, we’re looking for constructive stock charts. You don’t simply buy a stock because the chart looks good, but that’s definitely an important factor.

The takeaway is that investors may be able to find compelling growth opportunities even if the broader market continues to struggle with uncertainty surrounding the election and interest rates.

Dividend Stocks Offer Income Amid Market Uncertainty

Not every investor is looking to capitalize on a potential rally in growth stocks. For those who prefer a more income-oriented approach, dividend-paying stocks and ETFs can provide another way to participate in the market while collecting regular income.

Cabot Money Club Chief Analyst Nancy Zambell closely follows investor sentiment and sees reasons for optimism despite recent market volatility.

I keep track of what investors are doing in the market and how they’re feeling about it.

Right now, I’d say most everybody is a little challenged in the short term, but over the long term, they’re still very bullish. So I’m happy to report that.

Nancy also favors diversified investments that provide income, including dividend-paying ETFs.

While dividend stocks and ETFs aren’t immune to market declines, they can offer investors a way to remain invested and collect income without depending entirely on rising share prices.

And with uncertainty surrounding the midterm elections, that could be an appealing alternative for investors looking to balance growth opportunities with income.

4 Investment Opportunities for the Post-Election Market

The 2026 midterm elections are approaching, and the market backdrop is decidedly uncertain.

But, as highlighted by our analysts, there are reasons for optimism. Internal market weakness could give way to seasonal strength, bearish sentiment could reverse, improving corporate earnings could support individual stocks, and income investments could remain in favor.

While a post-election stock market rally may not be guaranteed, historical post-election trends favor the bulls, as do end-of-year seasonal patterns, but there will undoubtedly be winners and losers, however the market shapes up after midterms.

That’s why identifying the right opportunities is important.

In our October 22 webinar, 4 Stocks to Maximize Profits in a Post-Midterms Market, Clif Droke, Jacob Mintz, Tyler Laundon and Nancy Zambell go beyond their broader market outlooks to reveal four specific investment opportunities they’re watching for the months ahead.

Whether you’re looking for growth opportunities, turnaround candidates, income investments or ways to capitalize on changing market sentiment, you’ll hear their individual strategies and the reasoning behind their recommendations.

Watch the October 22 Webinar: 4 Stocks to Maximize Profits in a Post-Midterms Market

data.title: AI Buildout Enters Its Middle Stages: What It Means for Turnaround Investors
data.description:
It has long been my contention that the AI buildout—which unquestionably is the dominant force underlying the current market environment—will ensure abundant liquidity for equities for as long as it persists.

It can further be argued that the AI investment theme is today’s analog to the computer tech buildout of the 1980s or the Internet stock boom of the ‘90s and, as such, is doing much of the heavy lifting for the major indexes.

For the last couple of years, investors who were awake to this reality were able to operate more or less on cruise control, secure in the knowledge that AI-related liquidity would almost certainly support the tech sector through whatever geopolitical or economic obstacle might emerge along the way, specifically, the fact that the AI buildout was in its early innings and presumably had a long way to go before completion.

[text_ad]

This point cannot be understated, for it calls to mind the similar boom in tech stocks that dominated the mid-to-late 1990s during the Internet infrastructure buildout phase. In similar fashion, as long as the Internet buildout was in force, the Nasdaq had a solid backstop.

However, when the Internet buildout was largely complete (or was at least significantly advanced), that’s when the Internet stock boom ran into trouble. In a similar vein, I think we can assume that the current AI buildout will follow much the same path. That is, as long as the data center infrastructural development remains largely incomplete, stocks in the aggregate are likely to remain buoyant as the massive amounts of money flowing into AI-related themes should support the broader market.

The good news through much of this year is that it was universally assumed that AI development was still in its early stages. But it now appears the buildout has entered its intermediate phase. And while it still suggests liquidity should remain ample enough going forward, since the buildout isn’t yet in its advanced stages, it means the heady days of investors operating on cruise control are likely numbered. To wit, the low volatility environment that has persisted for much of this year is likely to give way to more volatility heading into 2027.

Again, this isn’t to say that a bear market is imminent. I maintain that bullish conditions, overall, are likely to persist well into next year. But if the AI buildout is indeed entering its middle stages, we can look to the computer tech and Internet stock buildout analogs of the past for clues to what we can likely expect from here.

Before discussing that, I need to point out my reasoning for assuming the AI buildout is entering its middle stage. The recent appearance of fear surrounding the pace of AI development is, I think, a major piece of evidence. Underscoring this concern was a post on the social media platform X that made news headlines when former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher Jason Coxon warned that AI labs are racing toward self-improving superintelligence and gambling with human lives.

His post sent shockwaves through the AI industry, as well as among investors, especially as its implication was that increased government regulation would be a likely next step. On that score, several leading AI companies and executives are now asking the federal government for more regulation or oversight of advanced AI. And that, in turn, can be taken as a sign that the big industry players are looking to weed out their smaller competitors as the AI buildout advances.

The AI Buildout vs. the Internet Buildout

This is not unlike what we saw during the ‘90s internet buildout boom when “wildcat” independent internet startups were nibbling at the heels of the bigger companies during the early phase of the boom, and in doing so, eating into their bigger competitors’ margins while also increasing concerns among federal regulators over internet security and consumer protection. The end result was that by the latter part of that decade, many of the smaller players were weeded out by the increased regulations that followed.

In a similar vein, I think a case can be made that then-Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan’s infamous “irrational exuberance” speech in December 1996 marked the start of the middle phase of the internet infrastructural buildout. And indeed, it was roughly from that time onward that tech sector volatility began to steadily increase as the buildout became more advanced and liquidity became less profuse while speculative excesses also became more pronounced.

Granted, there is a danger in extrapolating this analogy too far, particularly as concerns over the pace and risks of the AI buildout intensify. Yet the regulatory environment is also beginning to change: OpenAI, for example, has recently called for mandatory, capability-based federal AI safety requirements, including testing, independent assessments, cybersecurity protections and incident reporting. If such regulation gains momentum, it could eventually favor larger, better-capitalized players and contribute to consolidation within portions of the AI ecosystem.

Exploring the Next Stage of the AI Buildout

That in turn wouldn’t necessarily mean that AI infrastructure spending immediately declines; rather, the next phase could involve a gradual shift from rapid expansion and proliferation toward greater concentration, tighter capital discipline and a smaller number of dominant players. And that would almost certainly mean shrinking liquidity for capital markets as the final stages of the AI buildout approach.

I view this development (which almost certainly has a long way to go before it completely plays out) as being a double-edged sword for turnaround investors. On the one hand, the early stages of the AI buildout haven’t been entirely kind to turnaround stocks in certain sectors and industries—the exception, of course, being AI and infrastructure-related companies undergoing turnarounds, e.g., Intel (INTC).

But companies experiencing a financial turnaround that aren’t directly tech-facing have admittedly had a much tougher go of it this year. Investors seem content to focus their attention on AI and related spaces while largely ignoring “old economy” sectors, resulting in a great many turnaround stocks languishing as investment funds are allocated elsewhere.

Why the Middle Stages of the AI Buildout Should Favor Turnaround Investors

I believe that paradigm could change, however, as the middle phase of the AI buildout becomes more apparent to investors heading into 2027. And as tech sector volatility presumably increases, investors will be incentivized to turn their attention to the value-oriented aspects of the market, which in turn should benefit the largely ignored (non-tech-related) turnarounds.

That prediction would align with what happened starting in 1997 when the Internet buildout entered its middle phase and a sector rotation into utilities, biopharma and retail stocks began as a cooling of internet “mania” among investors was in evidence. By 1998, moreover, investors were increasingly sensitive to valuation and were actively hunting for bargains across a large number of non-tech sectors.

With that in mind, I think turnaround and deep-value investors can take heart: Patience is apt to be rewarded at some point during the second half of the AI buildout phase, which, by my reckoning, is now upon us.

[author_ad]

data.title: 3 High-Growth Big Bank Stocks Trading at a Discount
data.description:
In my near-constant search for the next stocks to add to my Cabot Value Investor portfolio, a useful screening tool I use is courtesy of finviz.com, short for “Financial Visualizations.” There, I screen for stocks with low price-to-earnings and price-to-sales ratios, with high earnings growth – typically north of 10% expected EPS growth in the current fiscal year.
Right now, a simple search using those parameters brings up a whole lot of banks.

Of the 20 largest companies by market cap that show up in my screen, half of them are financials. One prominent name is a stock I currently recommend to my Cabot Value Investor readers. Most of the others are household names as well and are appealing to various degrees. I like three of them in particular. All three big bank stocks possess the combination of growth and value that I seek when searching for undervalued opportunities ripe for a major (and immediate) bounce-back.

[text_ad]

Here they are, from largest to “smallest” by market cap.

These Big Bank Stocks Are on Sale

Citigroup (C)

Forward P/E: 10.20
Price-to-sales: 2.61
Estimated 2026 EPS growth: 51.8%

The third-largest U.S. bank by assets, Citigroup is coming off an impressive third quarter (reported last week) in which it grew earnings by 39.8% and revenue by 8%. The $2.83 in earnings per share topped the $2.63 estimate, and the $23.84 billion in revenue marked the bank’s third-best quarter in the last decade. And yet, shares have fallen by about 6% since the earnings report, likely because trading profits – while up 2% year over year – declined 27% from the previous quarter due to a drop in equity trading revenue. Investment banking revenue also declined 13% quarter over quarter, despite being up 9% year over year. I think those are flimsy reasons for C shares to sell off, as quarterly trading and investment banking are subject to the whims of the market environment, while yearly progress is a better gauge of strength. Overall, Citi’s growth on both the top (on track for 12.6% revenue growth this year) and bottom lines is stellar, and yet the stock is 15% below its June highs and is only up 5% year to date. I see the post-earnings selling as overdone and needless, and expect the stock to bounce back rather swiftly.

Banco Santander (SAN)

Forward P/E: 10.27
Price-to-sales: 3.00
Estimated 2026 EPS growth: 20.8%

Banco Santander is a Spain-based bank that is the fourth largest in Europe by assets, but an expanding U.S. footprint has contributed to accelerating growth of late. The company’s fast-growing digital banking wing, OpenBank, is a hit in America and has helped Santander double its earnings per share in the last five years (the low-overhead digital banking approach has allowed the bank to shutter some of its physical branches, namely in Europe, which has contributed to higher profits). As a result, the stock has performed quite well – up 38% in the last 12 months and nearly tripling since the start of 2025. However, because of the rapid earnings growth, the stock is still relatively cheap, trading at just 10.3x forward earnings – well below the 12.6x it was trading for in late 2025. One thing to note with this stock, though: Santander reports third-quarter earnings next Wednesday, October 28. So you might want to hold off on starting big positions until after those come out.

UBS Group (UBS)

Forward P/E: 11.64
Price-to-sales: 3.13
Estimated 2026 EPS growth: 13.3%

Another cheap large-cap European bank, UBS – a former holding in this portfolio under my predecessor Bruce Kaser – is just a steady growth machine, posting double-digit sales and earnings growth in the second quarter and on track for 14.4% revenue growth for the year and 13.3% earnings growth. Like Santander, the Swiss bank reports third-quarter results next Wednesday, October 28. But unlike SAN, UBS shares have not taken off this year, up a mere 2.7% year to date and trading 14% below their early-September highs. At just 11.6x forward earnings estimates, the stock trades well below its five-year average (15x). It’s not growing as fast as Santander or Citigroup, but it arguably has just as much – if not more – value.

Those are three of my favorite undervalued banks right now. The fact that such prominent names in the financial space are trading at such deep discounts speaks to how underappreciated the sector as a whole has been of late – even in a U.S. and global economy that’s still growing.

And, of course, to learn the name of the undervalued bank I’m currently recommending to my Cabot Value Investor readers, you can take out a subscription by clicking here.

data.title: The Inflation Nemesis—More Fed Rate Hikes Are Coming
data.description:
More Fed rate hikes are coming. Politics aside, they are going to honor their mandate. With inflation remaining stubbornly high and the economy showing few signs of weakness, the Fed has little choice but to keep raising interest rates.

Why More Fed Rate Hikes Are Needed

The central bank has a dual mandate that involves inflation and employment. When one becomes a problem, they need to act. If unemployment becomes a problem, they lower the fed funds rate to stimulate the economy. If inflation is the problem, they raise the rate to slow down the economy and push back against rising prices. How are things going now?

Employment isn’t a problem right now in any way, shape or form. In fact, the current unemployment rate is near the lowest level on record. At the same time, the economy is rock solid. The Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta currently estimates 3.5% GDP growth in the third quarter. If true, that will be the highest level of GDP growth since the pandemic recovery in 2022. It’s also well above the average level of economic growth over the past several decades.

The economy doesn’t need any help from the Fed. Inflation is a quite different story.

Why Inflation Is Still a Problem

Inflation went away as a problem from the early 1980s to the 2020s. The Consumer Price Index (CPI) began lower than 2% in 2020 after having averaged around 2% for decades. But the inflation rate exploded in the following years. The CPI went from under 2% in 2020 to over 9% by the middle of 2022. The rate did move down to around 3% before the recent spike. But the genie is out of the bottle.

These aren’t just a bunch of numbers for economics nerds to crunch. I’m sure you see it yourself. The prices of just about everything have gotten outrageous. By 2025, money was worth more than 20% less than it was just four years earlier. I bought two sandwiches at the deli the other day, nothing else, no chips or drinks. It cost $29. Are you kidding me?

I’ve morphed into my father. Apparently, I have some old-fashioned idea about what things should cost, and I’m still negatively surprised every time a bill comes due. I keep running around making outraged declarations like “twenty bucks?!”, just like Dad used to. It seems I’ve been transported to a world I don’t understand and don’t like. I know I’m weird, but I can’t be alone in this. I’ll bet you’re the same way.

[text_ad]

There are a couple of important things to understand about inflation. One is that the price increases are permanent; they never go back down. Sure, commodity items like food and gas prices do go up and down. But the general level of prices never decreases. That would be deflation. That hasn’t occurred since the Great Depression. Reduced inflation only means that prices increase from current levels at a slower pace.

Sticky Inflation Is Hard to Beat

The other thing to understand about inflation is that it’s a pain in the you-know-what. You can’t get rid of it without a deep recession or worse. This was obvious during the inflation of the 1970s. The Fed would jack up rates and wreck the economy to get inflation under control. It worked. But just for a while. As soon as the Fed took its foot off the gas, inflation came right back, worse than before. Inflation is like one of those annoying birthday candles that you can’t blow out.

Inflation, as measured by CPI, has come way down from the nosebleed levels earlier this decade. In fact, CPI averaged less than 3% from the middle of 2024 until early this year. But inflation has moved higher again since the Iran war, and ensuing higher oil prices, began in March. Since then, the monthly headline inflation rate has averaged 3.6%, well above the Fed’s mandated 2% level.

If you’re old like me, you probably remember the double-digit inflation of the late ‘70s and early ‘80s. Back then, we would have killed for 3.6% inflation. It seems like today we have a bunch of wussies whining about a little 3.6%. But it’s not the same. Inflation is measured differently than it was back then. By the same 1970s standards, the rate is much higher. And it is a problem.

Sure, the recent increase in inflation is largely due to the higher energy prices that have resulted from the conflict with Iran. It’s also likely that the conflict will end in the not-too-distant future and oil prices and inflation will come back down. But it will not come down to the Fed’s mandated level of 2%. No way. Not without a painful economic downturn.

The Fed Will Have to Raise Rates Again in 2026

Inflation is sticky. And it’s here to stay. The Fed will raise the fed funds rate again at least one more time this year, and probably more next year. They’ll have to raise the rate until a crummy economy lowers inflation. That’s the inflation conundrum.

The current high interest rates are not an aberration. It’s the new normal.

Get used to it and adjust accordingly.

data.title: How to Use 52-Week Highs and Lows to Gauge Market Strength
data.description:
Investing in an economically and geopolitically turbulent and politically charged environment is challenging, but using the right tools can drastically increase your odds of successfully navigating the stock market’s troubled waters. Here I’ll explain how using the new 52-week highs and lows will help you instantly locate the weakest segments of the market, while also helping you isolate areas of unusual strength.

When it comes to equity market investing, one of the most important concepts for investors to understand is that of relative strength. Relative strength is basically a gauge of how well a particular stock, industry or sector is performing compared with the broad market as measured by a benchmark average (such as the S&P 500 Index). By focusing on publicly traded shares that are in a relative strength position versus the S&P, you can be reasonably assured of improving your investment batting average over time.

While there are exceptions to the relative strength rule, the rule is fairly simple: Whenever a stock or stock group is conspicuously outperforming the S&P 500 for an extended period, it’s assumed that the “smart money” (e.g. institutional investors, hedge funds and/or corporate insiders) are actively involved in the stock(s) in question and have likely been accumulating shares. And it’s usually a good idea to follow the footsteps of these informed participants so that whatever stocks they own, you also want to own.

[text_ad]

What the 52-Week Highs Tell Us

There are many different methods for finding relative strength in the equity market, but one of the simplest and most effective ways is to monitor the daily number of stocks making new 52-week highs and lows. Both major U.S. exchanges publish these figures each day and they can be found on any number of websites for free (my favorite is the The Wall Street Journal’s list, which you can find here).

Whenever major averages like the S&P 500 are in an extended upward trend, many traders use the new 52-week highs for the NYSE and Nasdaq exchanges to quickly locate the stocks which stand the best chance of continuing to trend even higher. This is a momentum strategy, and although it’s not without pitfalls, it can be quite effective as long as bull market conditions prevail. That’s because stocks which consistently make new 52-week highs typically don’t face as much overhead supply or “chart resistance” (i.e., previous price peaks, which often serve as reversal areas for stocks). After all, it’s much easier for institutions to push stocks higher when there are no previous obstacles in the way.

CNBC’s Jim Cramer has observed, “As a voting machine, you cannot [beat] the new 52-week highs, and they do not get there for no reason.”

New 52-week highs have also been likened to baseball players who boast stellar batting averages (the players you want to bet on). Just as ball players on a hitting streak tend to continue outperforming, so, too, do the stocks which consistently make new highs—that is, as long as bullish broad market conditions prevail. And a bullish environment is usually characterized by new 52-week highs outnumbering new 52-week lows by at least a 3-to-1 ratio (the higher the better) on a daily basis.

What the 52-Week Lows Tell Us

This leads us to the other important aspect of the new highs and lows, namely how they can be used to quickly isolate areas of weakness. Whenever a general market uptrend shows signs of losing steam, one of the first places you should consult to see where most of the weakness is concentrated is the list of NYSE stocks making new 52-week lows.

The total number of listed stocks making new 52-week lows, while easy to gauge, contains a wealth of information in itself. The new lows tell us: 1.) if there’s an unusual degree of selling pressure within the market; and 2.) where exactly that selling pressure is located. Years ago, a study was made here at Cabot covering all stock market environments going back to 1962. That study found that:

“As long as the number of daily new lows did not exceed 40, the market was sound and in no danger of falling significantly. And remarkably, this specific threshold of 40 new lows remained the same over the entire 50 years we studied.”

This observation forms the basis of the Cabot Two Second Indicator, which is a daily determination of whether there are fewer than 40 stocks making new 52-week lows on the NYSE. If there are more than 40 new lows each day over a period of several consecutive days, you can be reasonably certain that there’s an abnormal degree of selling pressure somewhere in the market. And to isolate where exactly that selling pressure is coming from, all you have to do is pay attention to the stocks touching new lows; specifically, what sector or industry those stocks trade in.

(As an aside, this especially holds true during times in which the major averages are still in an uptrend, yet the new 52-week lows are increasing. It can almost always be assumed in such cases that the “smart money” is using the market’s surface strength to disguise their distribution, or selling activities.)

To illustrate the Two Second Indicator in action, let’s briefly examine the stock market’s latest internal profile.

In recent weeks, there has been a notable increase in the number of stocks making new 52-week lows on the NYSE. There are currently 93 NYSE stocks trading at 52-week lows, and just 54 making new highs.

As you can see in the chart below, the number of new lows has fallen from its recent peak but is still well above a “healthy” level, reflecting an ongoing correction under the surface of the headline indexes.

So, with new highs not meeting the 3-to-1 threshold mentioned earlier, we’re clearly not in bullish territory, despite some improvement in 52-week lows in recent days.

Once the new lows shrink to below 40 for several consecutive days, while new highs steadily increase (preferably to a 3-to-1 or greater ratio versus new lows), you can reasonably infer that sellers have been cleared out of the market and that the bulls are back in control of the dominant intermediate-term trend. But as long as there are 40 or more stocks making new 52-week lows each day, it’s generally a good idea to play it safe and avoid plunging back in.

As our growth investing expert Mike Cintolo has pointed out, “One of the big secrets to investing is to avoid making huge mistakes, and if you stay in gear with the trends and the action of the leaders, you’re guaranteed never to miss out on a major upmove or to stay bullish during a prolonged drop—and that fact alone puts you ahead of 80% of investors.”

Using the 52-week highs and lows to zero in on strength and avoid weakness will help you do just that.

If you want the best-performing growth stocks right now, I highly recommend subscribing to our Cabot Momentum Trader advisory, where every week Chief Analyst Mike Cintolo provides you with 10 of the market’s strongest growth stocks from both a technical and a fundamental perspective.

data.title: As Chip Stocks and Neoclouds Sell Off, “Everything Else” Catches a Bid
data.description:
Over the last two weeks, AI stocks have seen the most intense selling pressure since the collapse of hedge fund Situational Awareness in July.

Chip stocks, as measured by the iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX), fell 11.8% last week alone and were lower by 16.3% from their early-October highs at Friday’s close.

The neoclouds (companies whose business model is renting out computing power, or GPU-as-a-service) fared even worse, epitomized by the performance of CoreWeave (CRWV), which shed 25.2% in the last week and 31.5% in the last two.

And while concerns about the overall health of CoreWeave played a major role in the downturn (yields on the company’s bonds spiked to more than 15% at one point, a level that signals distress), peers Iren (IREN) and Nebius (NBIS) fared just as poorly, falling 44.4% and 33.8%, respectively, from their one-month highs.

But there’s a notable silver lining amidst all this selling. As pressure intensified in AI stocks, money simply rotated into other areas of the market.

[text_ad]

You can see that rotation clearly in the table below, which shows the five-day returns of all 11 S&P 500 sectors (as of the close on October 16).

The only notable decline in the last week was limited to Information Technology, while Consumer Staples, Energy, Health Care and Materials all logged impressive one-week returns.

There is, undoubtedly, a defensive bent to the repositioning, as Staples and Health Care are typically viewed as the most resilient sectors in a downturn, but the most important takeaway isn’t who outperformed last week but that any sectors outperformed at all.

Rather than liquidating high-flying AI names and fleeing to cash, big investors opted to stay invested and simply adjust their positioning, which is a signal that, for all the concerns about valuations, smart money sees exposure to equities as the best play heading into the heart of Q3 earnings season and then into the end of the year.

And given that staying on the same side of the market as smart money is normally a winning proposition, that’s instructive for individual investors as well.

That’s not to say that you should impulsively “buy the dip” at the first sign of selling (Monday’s bounce in tech names aside), but it’s a strong case for maintaining equity exposure.

Importantly, however you choose to invest in stocks, your investments should match your risk tolerance and time horizon. By maintaining a risk level you’re comfortable with, you can avoid making rash decisions while allowing “time in the market” to work in your favor.

That may mean trimming your allocation to high-growth tech stocks and buying small-cap stocks or dividend payers; or if you’re a more active investor, it may mean tightening up your stops.

Alternatively, if you’re looking for a bit more guidance, you may want to consider a subscription to Cabot Stock of the Week, where Chief Analyst Chris Preston identifies the best-looking stocks from a wide range of Cabot’s advisories to recommend the best of the best.

Because Stock of the Week isn’t limited to one style or sector, Chris is well-positioned to pounce on different areas of the market as they come into favor while maintaining the flexibility to rotate out of weak segments when they come under pressure.

Chris has flagged multiple double- and triple-digit winners already this year in areas as diverse as international banking, space-based communications, fiberoptics, semiconductors and health care.

data.title: Why Investing in Nordic Stocks Makes Sense Now
data.description:
The Nordic bloc of five countries and 30 million people is attracting the interest of investors for multiple surprising reasons.

Each of its countries, Sweden, Denmark, Norway, Finland and Iceland, has its own culture and take on politics, but what they share is more than a good vibe; it’s well-educated citizens, economic momentum, and savvy entrepreneurs. Sweden and Iceland have the highest numbers of tech “unicorns” outside the United States and Israel.

Long known for having generous socialistic states, the reality is quite different, as you can see from the debt map below, with the darker blue areas having less debt measured as a percentage of GDP.

The politics of government spending in the region is also changing with tougher rules on deficits, a more independent central bank, and national pension systems that adjust to longer lifespans.

[text_ad]

The bloc is also increasing its defense spending as Russia threatens its territory, China threatens its economic security, and as it must count less on America. They are integrating their economies, defense industries and militaries with each other and Europe.

Last year, Denmark and Norway each spent more than the U.S. on defense as a share of GDP, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.

The Nordic countries are closely tied to Germany, which leads the European NATO members in defense spending, as well as technology, manufacturing, and industry. I like Rheinmetall AG (RNMBY), which has strong order flow from the Ukraine conflict and NATO countries that are rebuilding their defense spending and industry. Rheinmetall remains at a sweet spot of growth, benefiting from higher NATO defense spending on ammunition, shipbuilding, electronics, unmanned systems and secure satellite communications.

The Stockholm Stock Exchange, also known as Nasdaq Stockholm, is the primary securities exchange of the Nordic countries. Founded in 1863, it is also a regional key hub for European capital markets.

Sweden has reduced public spending, cut the top marginal tax rates, and lowered taxes on property, gifts, wealth and inheritance. Sweden is bigger than Denmark and less state-dominated than Norway. Denmark has recently run surpluses, enabling the government to offer voters a hefty cut in electricity taxes.

Let’s focus on finance and economics to highlight Nordic power.

To begin, Sweden has about twice as many billionaires per capita as the U.S. and has a “stock culture,” with 22% of its citizens owning shares directly and – in contrast to our Social Security Trust Fund – a healthy allocation of stocks in its national pension plan. On the debt side, Sweden’s debt-to-GDP ratio is just above 35%, compared to America’s 102%. Not bad at all.

Denmark and Sweden, in particular, punch above their weight globally thanks to multinationals such as Denmark’s Novo (NVO) in weight-loss drugs, and Ørsted (DNNGY) in wind farms. Novo is now trading at a little more than 10 times earnings and offers us a return on equity of over 60% as well as ongoing share buybacks and pipeline flexibility.

Sweden offers Spotify (SPOT) in music streaming, and Saab (SAABY) in auto and defense, as well as H&M (HNNMY), Nordea Bank (NRDBY), Swedbank (SWDBY), and SKF (SKFRY).

Then there is the iShares MSCI Sweden ETF (EWD). This ETF is heavily weighted towards industrials at 45% of the basket, followed by financial services at 24%. It is fairly concentrated, with the top ten stocks comprising about 55% of its total value.

There is also an iShares MSCI Norway ETF (ENOR) that captures the dynamism of this booming energy and maritime country, reflected in this ETF’s tilt to oil and hydro energy and finance.
